requirements.requirement: Define political polarization and distinguish it from related outcomes such as ideological exposure, engagement, media diversity, political knowledge, partisan following, or general political activity.
requirements.description: The response should specify which forms of polarization are relevant—such as affective polarization, ideological extremity, partisan identity, or behavioral polarization—and should not treat changes in content exposure as polarization itself.

requirements.requirement: Evaluate whether recommendation or ranking algorithms change the political content users are shown.
requirements.description: The response should distinguish algorithmic ranking or recommendation effects from users’ follows, clicks, searches, subscriptions, and network composition, and should report relevant evidence on ideological slant, cross-cutting exposure, amplification, or content supply.

requirements.requirement: Evaluate whether algorithmically altered exposure causes changes in political beliefs, policy attitudes, partisan identity, or affective polarization.
requirements.description: The response should treat downstream attitudinal outcomes separately from feed composition and should characterize the direction, magnitude, statistical uncertainty, and substantive importance of reported effects.

requirements.requirement: Evaluate whether recommendation algorithms cause politically relevant behavioral changes.
requirements.description: Relevant outcomes may include voting, political participation, sharing, following, engagement, time spent, or other online and offline actions. The response should state when direct behavioral evidence is limited rather than inferring behavior from exposure or attitudes.

requirements.requirement: Distinguish the causal strength and limitations of the main types of evidence.
requirements.description: The response should differentiate randomized feed interventions, reranking experiments, audits, observational studies, surveys, and simulations, and should identify material threats such as self-selection, network or content-supply confounding, noncompliance, treatment contamination, and measurement error.

requirements.requirement: Compare results across platforms, interventions, populations, political contexts, and study settings.
requirements.description: The response should explain why findings from real-world feeds, chronological substitutions, reranking treatments, audits, and simulated environments may differ, while addressing relevant differences in country, language, election timing, user composition, and platform design.

requirements.requirement: Assess whether effects vary across users, content, outcomes, exposure intensity, and time horizons.
requirements.description: The response should consider subgroup differences, cumulative or persistent effects, feedback loops, changing algorithms, and external validity, while distinguishing evidence-supported heterogeneity from speculative mechanisms or claims about long-term accumulation.

requirements.requirement: Explain why the literature reaches different conclusions and provide a calibrated overall assessment of the extent to which algorithms contribute to polarization.
requirements.description: The response should connect disagreements to differences in constructs, designs, interventions, samples, contexts, statistical power, and effect-size thresholds. Its conclusion should separately characterize evidence for exposure changes and evidence for changes in beliefs or behavior, preserve uncertainty and scope conditions, and avoid overstating either negligible or substantial effects.
